input.question: Salts are constantly added to the ocean through volcanic emissions, runoff from continents, and the weathering of rocks in general, but is there any process that reverses this and removes it?
input.ground_truth: Yes. Salt can settle out, be captured by organic processes, and (most commonly) become landlocked. In that last one, a part of the ocean recedes or gets cut off from the rest of the ocean. The water evaporates and deposits the salt (which gets buried over time), then the fresh water rains back into the rest of the ocean.

Sure! Let’s make it simple:

**Question:**  
We always put salt in the ocean, like from volcanoes and rocks breaking down. But does anything ever take salt out of the ocean?

**Simple Answer:**  
Yes! Sometimes, salt can leave the ocean. One way is when the water in the ocean evaporates (turns into vapor and goes up into the sky as clouds), but the salt stays behind. Also, tiny sea creatures with shells, like snails and clams, use some of the salt to build their shells. When they die, their shells can sink to the bottom of the ocean or turn into rock, taking the salt with them. So, salt can leave the ocean in different ways!
